title: Rules or Character? Where to Spend Your Safety Budget
hook: Filters block bad outputs at inference; RLHF shapes behavior at training. A formal model asks how to split the budget — and finds scale matters far less than one parameter.
key_points: Frames safety design as a single allocation alpha in [0,1] between character shaping (RLHF, Constitutional AI) and rule enforcement (output filters, safety classifiers).
The model incorporates scale-dependent filter degradation, common-mode failures, and 'character fragility' — the risk that shaped behavior collapses under novel conditions.
The optimal split is interior or at the rules-only boundary, and shifts weakly toward character shaping as deployment scale T grows.
That shift ranges from negligible (+0.01) to pronounced (+0.21) depending on scenario — optimistic, moderate, or pessimistic.
The dominant parameter is baseline character fragility, which moves the optimum by 0.50 across its range — far more than tail severity, filter quality, or common-mode failure probability.
Takeaway: safety architecture depends less on deployment scale than on how reliably character shaping survives distributional shift.
content_html: Real safety stacks combine two very different instruments. Character shaping — RLHF, Constitutional AI — changes the behavioral distribution at training time. Rule enforcement — output filters, safety classifiers — blocks harmful outputs at inference. Everyone runs both, and there has been little formal analysis of how the balance should shift as deployment grows.
extra_html:
Takahashi and colleagues build a stylized comparative-statics model that reduces the choice to one allocation parameter, alpha in [0,1], while accounting for the ways each side fails: filters degrade as scale rises, both mechanisms can fail in common mode, and shaped character can be fragile — degrading or collapsing under conditions it was never shaped for. Under a multiplicative Pareto damage model they derive expected harm in closed form and add tail-risk (CVaR) analysis by Monte Carlo.

Two results stand out. The optimum does drift toward character shaping as deployment scale grows, but weakly — from +0.01 in the optimistic scenario to +0.21 in the pessimistic one, and sometimes sitting right at the rules-only boundary. What actually dominates is baseline character fragility, which moves the optimum by 0.50 across its plausible range, dwarfing tail severity, filter quality, and common-mode failure probability. So the authors' conclusion inverts the intuitive framing: how you architect safety should depend less on how widely you deploy than on how much you trust shaped behavior to survive distributional shift. It's a stylized model with assumed damage distributions, not an empirical study — useful for structuring the argument rather than for setting a number.

flashcards.prompt: In this model, which parameter most strongly determines the optimal rules-vs-character split?

choices.text: Baseline character fragility — it shifts the optimum by 0.50 across its range
Deployment scale, which dominates all other considerations
Tail severity of the harm distribution

flashcards.explanation_html: Fragility's effect (0.50) far exceeds that of tail severity, filter quality, or common-mode failure probability. Scale shifts the optimum only weakly, by +0.01 to +0.21 depending on scenario.

flashcards.back_html: The risk that behavior instilled at training time — via RLHF or Constitutional AI — degrades or collapses under novel conditions, i.e. under distributional shift away from what shaping covered.

flashcards.prompt: What's the practical conclusion for someone choosing between filters and training-time shaping?
flashcards.back_html: Don't decide from deployment scale. Decide from how reliably your shaped behavior holds under distributional shift — that's the parameter the optimum is actually sensitive to.
